entries.name: Combat (introduction)

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / p. 13

entries.evidence: Adventurers encounter many dangerous monsters and nefarious villains. In those moments, combat often breaks out.
entries.note: Read and declined: scene-setting prose that states no rule. It demands nothing of an engine.

entries.name: Combat as a cycle of rounds and turns

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / The Order of Combat / p. 13

ambiguity.question: This passage says the fight continues to the next round whenever neither side is defeated, while 'Ending Combat' says combat can also end when both sides agree to end it. Read literally, a combat in which both sides agree to stop but neither is defeated both continues (here) and ends (there). Which governs?

entries.evidence: A typical combat encounter is a clash between two sides: a flurry of weapon swings, feints, parries, footwork, and spellcasting. The game organizes combat into a cycle of rounds and turns. A round represents about 6 seconds in the game world. During a round, each participant in a battle takes a turn. The order of turns is determined at the beginning of combat when everyone rolls Initiative. Once everyone has taken a turn, the fight continues to the next round if neither side is defeated.
entries.note: The phase rule for combat: every turn-scoped entry in this slice names it in enabledBy. Whether combat has started is a fact the caller supplies (a parameter, no entry). The 'about 6 seconds' round length is mapped separately as combat-round-duration. Demonstrate: every participant takes exactly one turn per round; a new round starts only after all have had a turn.

entries.name: Length of a round

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / The Order of Combat / p. 13

ambiguity.question: 'About 6 seconds' does not fix the length of a round. Whether an engine may convert between rounds and game-world time as exactly 6 seconds per round (e.g. for durations stated in minutes) is not settled by this sentence.

entries.evidence: A round represents about 6 seconds in the game world.
entries.note: Prior knowledge pulls towards '10 rounds = 1 minute'; this slice does not say that, and 'about' was left open rather than read as exact.

entries.name: Combat step 1: Establish Positions

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / The Order of Combat / Combat Step by Step / p. 13

entries.evidence: 1: Establish Positions. The Game Master determines where all the characters and monsters are located. Given the adventurers’ marching order or their stated positions in the room or other location, the GM figures out where the adversaries are—how far away and in what direction.
entries.note: Gate 3: the Game Master's own determination is operative, and the same constituent states what it is measured against: 'Given the adventurers' marching order or their stated positions in the room or other location'. The GM is treated as the engine's caller (see MAPPER-NOTES). The engine demands the positions, attributes them to the GM, records them, and never infers them.

entries.name: Combat steps 2-3: Roll Initiative, Take Turns

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / The Order of Combat / Combat Step by Step / p. 13

entries.evidence: 2: Roll Initiative. Everyone involved in the combat encounter rolls Initiative, determining the order of combatants’ turns. 3: Take Turns. Each participant in the battle takes a turn in Initiative order. When everyone involved in the combat has had a turn, the round ends. Repeat this step until the fighting stops.
entries.note: 'Until the fighting stops' is read as pointing at 'Ending Combat' (no pointer phrase, so no crossReference). Demonstrate the order: positions, then Initiative once, then repeated rounds of turns in Initiative order.

entries.name: Rolling Initiative

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / The Order of Combat / Initiative / p. 13

entries.evidence: Initiative determines the order of turns during combat. When combat starts, every participant rolls Initiative; they make a Dexterity check that determines their place in the Initiative order. The GM rolls for monsters.
entries.note: Every participant makes a Dexterity check once, when combat starts; the GM rolls for monsters (attribution of who rolls, not a delegated judgement). Other passages outside the slice modify this roll (Incapacitated and Invisible conditions in the Rules Glossary); they are not mapped here.

entries.name: One Initiative roll for a group of identical creatures

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / The Order of Combat / Initiative / p. 13

ambiguity.question: Neither 'group' nor 'identical creatures' is defined: which creatures form a group that shares one roll (same stat block? acting together? the GM's choice?) is not fixed, and the passage names no one who fixes it by a stated measure.

entries.evidence: For a group of identical creatures, the GM makes a single roll, so each member of the group has the same Initiative.
entries.note: Prior knowledge suggests 'same stat block'; the text does not say so.

entries.name: Surprise: Disadvantage on Initiative

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / The Order of Combat / Initiative / p. 13

ambiguity.question: The slice says what being surprised does but defines 'surprised' only by one example (an ambusher hidden from a foe unaware that combat is starting). Whether any other situation makes a combatant surprised is not fixed, and no one is named to decide it. (The Rules Glossary's 'Surprise' entry, p. 189, says 'caught unawares by the start of combat', which is itself an undefined degree.)

entries.evidence: Surprise. If a combatant is surprised by combat starting, that combatant has Disadvantage on their Initiative roll. For example, if an ambusher starts combat while hidden from a foe who is unaware that combat is starting, that foe is surprised.
entries.note: The effect (Disadvantage on the Initiative roll) is clear; the ambiguity is the trigger. Demonstrate that a surprised combatant still rolls and still takes turns.

entries.name: Initiative count

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / The Order of Combat / Initiative / p. 13

entries.evidence: A combatant’s check total is called their Initiative count, or Initiative for short.
entries.note: A definition: the vocabulary initiative-order and mount-controlled-initiative use.

entries.name: Initiative order

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / The Order of Combat / Initiative / p. 13

entries.evidence: The GM ranks the combatants, from highest to lowest Initiative. This is the order in which they act during each round. The Initiative order remains the same from round to round.
entries.note: Highest acts first; order fixed across rounds. suspendedBy mount-controlled-initiative because a controlled mount's Initiative 'changes to match yours', which departs from 'remains the same from round to round' for that mount only (the gate is entry-level; the reach is that one combatant). Ties are initiative-ties.

entries.name: Initiative ties

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / The Order of Combat / Initiative / p. 13

ambiguity.question: The corpus fixes who orders ties among monsters, among 'characters', and between 'a monster and a player character', but not: (a) what happens when the players whose characters are tied do not agree; (b) whether 'characters' includes characters that are not player characters, and who orders a tie between a monster and such a character.

entries.evidence: Ties. If a tie occurs, the GM decides the order among tied monsters, and the players decide the order among tied characters. The GM decides the 13 System Reference Document 5.2.1 order if the tie is between a monster and a player character.
entries.note: Gate 3, delegated-choice arm: the GM's or players' choice is operative and the set of values is fixed in the same constituent ('the order among tied monsters' / 'among tied characters', i.e. an ordering of the tied combatants). The span crosses the page-13 footer ('13 System Reference Document 5.2.1') in the extraction; on the printed page the sentence continues at the top of the right-hand column.

entries.name: Your turn: move and one action

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / The Order of Combat / Your Turn / p. 13

entries.evidence: On your turn, you can move a distance up to your Speed and take one action. You decide whether to move first or take your action first.
entries.note: Demonstrate both orders (move then act, act then move). Incapacitated removes the action half only; the gate is not recorded on this entry because it does not suspend the move (see MAPPER-NOTES).

entries.name: Where action options come from

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / The Order of Combat / Your Turn / p. 13

crossReferences.cites: listed in “Actions” earlier in “Playing the Game.”
“Movement and Position” later in “Playing the Game” gives the rules for movement

entries.evidence: The main actions you can take are listed in “Actions” earlier in “Playing the Game.” A character’s features and a monster’s stat block also provide action options. “Movement and Position” later in “Playing the Game” gives the rules for movement.
entries.note: A pointer passage: the set of actions is the Actions table plus features and stat blocks, which are outside the slice.

entries.name: Brief communication is free

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / The Order of Combat / Your Turn / p. 13

ambiguity.question: Where 'brief utterances and gestures' end and 'extended communication' (which requires an action) begins is not fixed; the corpus gives only examples of each ('a detailed explanation of something or an attempt to persuade a foe').

entries.evidence: Communicating. You can communicate however you are able—through brief utterances and gestures—as you take your turn. Doing so uses neither your action nor your move.
entries.note: Same question as communicate-extended; it is a gap between two stated classes, not a contradiction, so no conflict slug.

entries.name: Extended communication requires an action

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / The Order of Combat / Your Turn / p. 13

ambiguity.question: Where 'brief utterances and gestures' end and 'extended communication' begins is not fixed; only examples are given.

entries.evidence: Extended communication, such as a detailed explanation of something or an attempt to persuade a foe, requires an action. The Influence action is the main way you try to influence a monster.
entries.note: 'The Influence action is the main way you try to influence a monster' is kept in the span as a pointer to the Influence action (Rules Glossary), which is not mapped: the sentence says 'main way', not that persuasion must use it.

entries.name: One free object interaction

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / The Order of Combat / Your Turn / p. 13

entries.evidence: Interacting with Things. You can interact with one object or feature of the environment for free, during either your move or action. For example, you could open a door during your move as you stride toward a foe.
entries.note: One free interaction per turn, during the move or the action. Suspended for a particular object by an item that always requires an action, and by a GM requirement.

entries.name: A second interaction needs the Utilize action

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / The Order of Combat / Your Turn / p. 13

entries.evidence: If you want to interact with a second object, you need to take the Utilize action.
entries.note: Demonstrate: first interaction free, second costs the Utilize action.

entries.name: Objects that always require an action

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / The Order of Combat / Your Turn / p. 13

crossReferences.unmapped: Item and object descriptions (e.g. 'Magic Items') are outside this slice; the requirement is data an item supplies, not a passage in the slice.

entries.evidence: Some magic items and other special objects always require an action to use, as stated in their descriptions.
entries.note: Which objects are such is supplied by each object's description.

entries.name: GM may require an action for an interaction

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / The Order of Combat / Your Turn / p. 14

ambiguity.question: 'Any of these activities' has no explicit antecedent. On the printed page it follows the 'Interacting with Things' paragraphs (in the extraction the 'Playing on a Grid' sidebar falls between them), so it plausibly means object interactions, but it could also take in the free communication described earlier under 'Your Turn'.

entries.evidence: The GM might require you to use an action for any of these activities when it needs special care or when it presents an unusual obstacle. For instance, the GM might require you to take the Utilize action to open a stuck door or turn a crank to lower a drawbridge.
entries.note: Gate 3: the GM's determination is operative and the constituent states its measure: 'when it needs special care or when it presents an unusual obstacle'. Heading: the passage continues 'Your Turn' from p. 13 (printed page top-left of p. 14).

entries.name: Doing nothing on your turn

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / The Order of Combat / Your Turn / p. 14

entries.evidence: Doing Nothing on Your Turn. You can forgo moving, taking an action, or doing anything at all on your turn.
entries.note: The advice in the following sentence is mapped separately as doing-nothing-advice (declined).

entries.name: Advice: Dodge or Ready if undecided

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / The Order of Combat / Your Turn / p. 14

entries.evidence: If you can’t decide what to do, consider taking the defensive Dodge action or the Ready action to delay acting.
entries.note: Advice, not a rule ('consider'); dropped and recorded here so it is not mistaken for a silent omission.

entries.name: Grid rules apply when playing on a grid

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / The Order of Combat / Playing on a Grid / p. 13

entries.evidence: If you play using a square grid and miniatures or other tokens, follow these rules.
entries.note: The gate for every grid entry: whether the table plays on a square grid is a caller-supplied parameter. The sidebar sits in the right column of p. 13; its placement under 'Your Turn' in the heading path follows the page layout.

entries.name: Each square is 5 feet

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / The Order of Combat / Playing on a Grid / p. 13

entries.evidence: Squares. Each square represents 5 feet.

entries.name: Speed in squares

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / The Order of Combat / Playing on a Grid / p. 13

ambiguity.question: Dividing Speed by 5 is stated without saying what happens to a remainder (a Speed that is not a multiple of 5, e.g. after halving): whether it is rounded down under the general 'Round Down' rule (p. 5) or leftover feet are usable is not stated here.

entries.evidence: Speed. Rather than moving foot by foot, move square by square on the grid, using your Speed in 5-foot segments. You can translate your Speed into squares by dividing it by 5. For example, a Speed of 30 feet translates into 6 squares.
entries.note: Prior knowledge suggests rounding down; the passage does not say it, and the general 'Round Down' rule speaks of dividing a number, which may settle it, so the question is left for Phase 4.

entries.name: Advice: write Speed in squares

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / The Order of Combat / Playing on a Grid / p. 13

entries.evidence: If you use a grid often, consider writing your Speed in squares on your character sheet.
entries.note: Advice, dropped.

entries.name: Cost to enter a square

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / The Order of Combat / Playing on a Grid / p. 13

ambiguity.question: The passage prices an unoccupied adjacent square (1) and a square of Difficult Terrain (2), but not a square occupied by a creature whose space is not Difficult Terrain for you (an ally, or a Tiny creature), which the 'Moving around Other Creatures' rules let you pass through. The case is not fixed.

entries.evidence: Entering a Square. To enter a square, you must have enough movement left to pay for entering. It costs 1 square of movement to enter an unoccupied square that’s adjacent to your space (orthogonally or diagonally adjacent). A square of Difficult Terrain costs 2 squares to enter. Other effects might make a square cost even more.
entries.note: Diagonal adjacency costs the same as orthogonal (stated). 'Other effects might make a square cost even more' points to unnamed effects; no pointer phrase.

entries.name: Diagonal movement and corners

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / The Order of Combat / Playing on a Grid / p. 13

entries.evidence: Corners. Diagonal movement can’t cross the corner of a wall, a large tree, or another terrain feature that fills its space.
entries.note: Whether a terrain feature fills its space is a fact of the map (parameter).

entries.name: Counting range on a grid

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / The Order of Combat / Playing on a Grid / p. 13

ambiguity.question: 'Count by the shortest route' does not say whether the route must go around walls and other obstacles (and Corners) or is a straight count of squares ignoring them, nor restates whether a diagonal step counts as one square for range as it does for movement.

entries.evidence: Ranges. To determine the range on a grid between two things—whether creatures or objects— count squares from a square adjacent to one of them and stop counting in the space of the other one. Count by the shortest route.
entries.note: Prior knowledge pulls toward 'diagonals count as 5 feet, obstacles ignored'; the passage is silent on both.

entries.name: A diagonal step on a grid costs 5 feet of Speed
entries.note: grid-entering-square says entering a diagonally adjacent unoccupied square costs 1 square of movement; grid-square-size says a square represents 5 feet. Together: a diagonal step costs 5 feet of Speed, the same as an orthogonal one. No sentence states the diagonal cost in feet.

entries.name: Combat ends when a side is defeated

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / The Order of Combat / Ending Combat / p. 14

ambiguity.question: 'Defeated' is illustrated ('can mean the creatures are killed or knocked out or have surrendered or fled') rather than defined: whether a side is defeated when only some of its creatures are, or in a situation not listed, is not fixed, and nobody is named to decide.

entries.evidence: Combat ends when one side or the other is defeated, which can mean the creatures are killed or knocked out or have surrendered or fled.
entries.note: A gate: it suspends every combat-phase entry. The conflict with combat-rounds-and-turns is about the agreement clause (combat-end-agreement), not this one.

entries.name: Combat ends by agreement

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / The Order of Combat / Ending Combat / p. 14

ambiguity.question: This says combat can end when both sides agree; 'The Order of Combat' says the fight continues to the next round if neither side is defeated. Which governs when both sides agree and neither is defeated?

entries.evidence: Combat can also end when both sides agree to end it.
entries.note: Whether both sides agree is a fact the rule tests (gate 1 parameter). A gate on every combat-phase entry.

entries.name: Move up to your Speed

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / Movement and Position / p. 14

entries.evidence: On your turn, you can move a distance equal to your Speed or less. Or you can decide not to move.
entries.note: Restates the move half of turn-move-and-action consistently.

entries.name: Climbing, crawling, jumping, swimming as part of a move

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / Movement and Position / p. 14

entries.evidence: Your movement can include climbing, crawling, jumping, and swimming (each explained in “Rules Glossary”). These different modes of movement can be combined with your regular movement, or they can constitute your entire move.
entries.note: One pointer ('each explained in "Rules Glossary"') reaching four glossary entries; declared once per term.

entries.name: Deducting movement from Speed

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / Movement and Position / p. 14

entries.evidence: However you’re moving with your Speed, you deduct the distance of each part of your move from it until it is used up or until you are done moving, whichever comes first.
entries.note: Demonstrate a move split into parts using different modes, each part deducted from the same Speed.

entries.name: Where Speed comes from

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / Movement and Position / p. 14

crossReferences.cites: See “Rules Glossary” for more about Speed

crossReferences.unmapped: Character creation is outside this slice; Speed reaches the engine as a caller-supplied parameter.

entries.evidence: A character’s Speed is determined during character creation. A monster’s Speed is noted in the monster’s stat block. See “Rules Glossary” for more about Speed as well as about special speeds, such as a Climb Speed, Fly Speed, or Swim Speed.
entries.note: Speed itself is a parameter (from character creation or stat block).

entries.name: What Difficult Terrain is

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / Movement and Position / Difficult Terrain / p. 14

ambiguity.question: The slice gives only examples of Difficult Terrain ('Low furniture, rubble, undergrowth, steep stairs, snow, and shallow bogs'); what else counts is not fixed here and no one is named to decide. (The Rules Glossary's list, p. 181, ends 'or something similar' and is outside the slice.)

entries.evidence: Combatants are often slowed down by Difficult Terrain. Low furniture, rubble, undergrowth, steep stairs, snow, and shallow bogs are examples of Difficult Terrain.
entries.note: Another creature's space is Difficult Terrain by other-creature-space-difficult, which is stated and needs no judgement.

entries.name: Movement cost in Difficult Terrain

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / Movement and Position / Difficult Terrain / p. 14

entries.evidence: Every foot of movement in Difficult Terrain costs 1 extra foot, even if multiple things in a space count as Difficult Terrain.
entries.note: Demonstrate that overlapping sources of Difficult Terrain still cost only 1 extra foot per foot.

entries.name: Breaking up your move

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / Movement and Position / Breaking Up Your Move / p. 14

entries.evidence: You can break up your move, using some of its movement before and after any action, Bonus Action, or Reaction you take on the same turn. For example, if you have a Speed of 30 feet, you could go 10 feet, take an action, and then go 20 feet.

entries.name: Dropping Prone

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / Movement and Position / Dropping Prone / p. 14

entries.evidence: On your turn, you can give yourself the Prone condition (see “Rules Glossary”) without using an action or any of your Speed, but you can’t do so if your Speed is 0.
entries.note: Free (no action, no Speed), barred at Speed 0. Demonstrate both.

entries.name: Size categories and space

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / Movement and Position / Creature Size / p. 14

crossReferences.cites: as shown on the Creature Size and Space table

entries.evidence: A creature belongs to a size category, which determines the width of the square space the creature occupies on a map, as shown on the Creature Size and Space table. That table lists the sizes from smallest (Tiny) to largest (Gargantuan).
entries.note: Fixes the order of sizes, which 'two sizes larger or smaller' and 'of a larger size' consume.

entries.name: What a creature's space is

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / Movement and Position / Creature Size / p. 14

entries.evidence: A creature’s space is the area that it effectively controls in combat and the area it needs to fight effectively.
entries.note: A definition; descriptive, with the operative measure in size-space-table.

entries.name: Where size comes from

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / Movement and Position / Creature Size / p. 14

entries.evidence: A character’s size is determined by species, and a monster’s size is specified in the monster’s stat block.
entries.note: Size is a caller-supplied parameter.

entries.name: Creature Size and Space table

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / Movement and Position / Creature Size / p. 14

entries.evidence: Creature Size and Space Size Space (Feet) Space (Squares) Tiny 2½ by 2½ feet 4 per square Small 5 by 5 feet 1 square Medium 5 by 5 feet 1 square Large 10 by 10 feet 4 squares (2 by 2) Huge 15 by 15 feet 9 squares (3 by 3) Gargantuan 20 by 20 feet 16 squares (4 by 4)
entries.note: The whole table, all six rows: Tiny 2½ by 2½ feet / 4 per square; Small and Medium 5 by 5 / 1 square; Large 10 by 10 / 4 squares (2 by 2); Huge 15 by 15 / 9 squares (3 by 3); Gargantuan 20 by 20 / 16 squares (4 by 4). Transcription must be verified against every row.

entries.name: Passing through other creatures' spaces

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / Movement and Position / Moving around Other Creatures / p. 14

ambiguity.question: (a) 'A creature that is two sizes larger or smaller than you' does not say whether exactly two sizes or at least two sizes is meant (e.g. Tiny passing through Huge, three sizes apart). (b) The passage grants permission for four cases and does not say whether the space of any other creature (e.g. a hostile creature one size apart) can be passed through.

entries.evidence: During your move, you can pass through the space of an ally, a creature that has the Incapacitated condition (see “Rules Glossary”), a Tiny creature, or a creature that is two sizes larger or smaller than you.
entries.note: Prior knowledge (an earlier edition's 'at least two sizes' and 'you can't move through a hostile creature's space') pulls at both halves; neither is in this text.

entries.name: Another creature's space is Difficult Terrain

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / Movement and Position / Moving around Other Creatures / p. 14

entries.evidence: Another creature’s space is Difficult Terrain for you unless that creature is Tiny or your ally.

entries.name: Passing through a larger or smaller non-ally costs extra movement
entries.note: move-through-space lets you pass through a creature two sizes larger or smaller (and an Incapacitated creature); other-creature-space-difficult makes its space Difficult Terrain unless it is Tiny or your ally. So passing through such a creature that is neither Tiny nor an ally is permitted and costs 1 extra foot per foot. No sentence states the combination.

entries.name: Can't willingly end a move in an occupied space

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / Movement and Position / Moving around Other Creatures / p. 14

entries.evidence: You can’t willingly end a move in a space occupied by another creature.
entries.note: 'Willingly' is a fact the rule tests (parameter).

entries.name: Ending a turn in another creature's space

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / Movement and Position / Moving around Other Creatures / p. 14

entries.evidence: If you somehow end a turn in a space with another creature, you have the Prone condition (see “Rules Glossary”) unless you are Tiny or are of a larger size than the other creature.
entries.note: Note the corpus says 'end a move' in the preceding sentence and 'end a turn' here; they are mapped as two rules. Demonstrate Tiny and larger-size exemptions.

entries.name: What lets you make an attack

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / Making an Attack / p. 14

entries.evidence: When you take the Attack action, you make an attack. Some other actions, Bonus Actions, and Reactions also let you make an attack.
entries.note: Which other actions, Bonus Actions and Reactions allow an attack is supplied by those features (outside the slice).

entries.name: The structure of an attack

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / Making an Attack / p. 15

entries.evidence: or make an attack roll as part of a spell, an attack has the following structure:
entries.note: The sentence begins on p. 14 ('Whether you strike with a Melee weapon, fire a Ranged weapon,'); the extraction places the 'Unseen Attackers and Targets' sidebar between the halves, so the span quotes the p. 15 half only. It applies to weapon attacks, and to attack rolls made as part of a spell.

entries.name: Attack step 1: Choose a Target

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / Making an Attack / p. 15

entries.evidence: 1: Choose a Target. Pick a target within your attack’s range: a creature, an object, or a location.

entries.name: Attack step 2: Determine Modifiers

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / Making an Attack / p. 15

entries.evidence: 2: Determine Modifiers. The GM determines whether the target has Cover (see the next section) and whether you have Advantage or Disadvantage against the target. In addition, spells, special abilities, and other effects can apply penalties or bonuses to your attack roll.
entries.note: The GM's cover determination is the assertion cover-degree-determination, whose measure is in the Cover table; this step consumes it. Whether Advantage or Disadvantage applies is decided by the rules that grant them.

entries.name: Attack step 3: Resolve the Attack

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / Making an Attack / p. 15

crossReferences.cites: as detailed earlier in “Playing the Game.”

entries.evidence: 3: Resolve the Attack. Make the attack roll, as detailed earlier in “Playing the Game.” On a hit, you roll damage unless the particular attack has rules that specify otherwise. Some attacks cause special effects in addition to or instead of damage.
entries.note: Damage is rolled on a hit unless the attack's own rules say otherwise; damage rules begin after this slice.

entries.name: Attacking a target you can't see

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / Making an Attack / Unseen Attackers and Targets / p. 14

entries.evidence: When you make an attack roll against a target you can’t see, you have Disadvantage on the roll. This is true whether you’re guessing the target’s location or targeting a creature you can hear but not see.

entries.name: Targeting the wrong location misses

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / Making an Attack / Unseen Attackers and Targets / p. 14

entries.evidence: If the target isn’t in the location you targeted, you miss.

entries.name: Attacking a creature that can't see you

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / Making an Attack / Unseen Attackers and Targets / p. 14

entries.evidence: When a creature can’t see you, you have Advantage on attack rolls against it.

entries.name: Attacking while hidden gives away your location

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / Making an Attack / Unseen Attackers and Targets / p. 14

entries.evidence: If you are hidden when you make an attack roll, you give away your location when the attack hits or misses.
entries.note: Being hidden is established by the Hide action (Rules Glossary), which is the gate that makes this reachable.

entries.name: Cover and its degrees

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / Cover / p. 15

crossReferences.cites: As detailed in the Cover table

entries.evidence: Walls, trees, creatures, and other obstacles can provide cover, making a target more difficult to harm. As detailed in the Cover table, there are three degrees of cover, each of which gives a different benefit to a target.

entries.name: Cover only against effects from the far side

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / Cover / p. 15

entries.evidence: A target can benefit from cover only when an attack or other effect originates on the opposite side of the cover.
entries.note: Which side an effect originates on is a geometric fact (parameter).

entries.name: Only the most protective degree of cover applies

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / Cover / p. 15

entries.evidence: If a target is behind multiple sources of cover, only the most protective degree of cover applies; the degrees aren’t added together. For example, if a target is behind a creature that gives Half Cover and a tree trunk that gives Three-Quarters Cover, the target has Three-Quarters Cover.
entries.note: Demonstrate Half + Three-Quarters = Three-Quarters, never +7.

entries.name: Cover table: benefits

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / Cover / p. 15

ambiguity.question: Total Cover's benefit is 'Can't be targeted directly'. What counts as targeting 'directly', and so which effects still reach a target with Total Cover, is not fixed in the slice.

entries.name: What a ranged attack is

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / Ranged Attacks / p. 15

entries.evidence: When you make a ranged attack, you fire a bow, hurl an axe, or otherwise send projectiles to strike a foe at a distance. Many spells also involve making a ranged attack.
entries.note: Vocabulary. Whether a given attack is ranged is supplied by the weapon or spell.

entries.name: Ranged attacks only within range

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / Ranged Attacks / Range / p. 15

entries.evidence: You can make ranged attacks only against targets within a specified range. If a ranged attack, such as one made with a spell, has a single range, you can’t attack a target beyond this range.

entries.name: Normal and long range

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / Ranged Attacks / Range / p. 15

entries.evidence: Some ranged attacks, such as those made with a Longbow, have two ranges. The smaller number is the normal range, and the larger number is the long range. Your attack roll has Disadvantage when your target is beyond normal range, and you can’t attack a target beyond long range.
entries.note: Demonstrate: within normal range no penalty; beyond normal and within long, Disadvantage; beyond long, no attack. suspendedBy underwater-ranged, which replaces the long-range rule for weapon attacks underwater (beyond normal range auto-misses). The span follows the p. 15 footer in the extraction and is still p. 15.

entries.name: Ranged attacks in close combat

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / Ranged Attacks / Ranged Attacks in Close Combat / p. 15

entries.evidence: Aiming a ranged attack is more difficult when a foe is next to you. When you make a ranged attack roll with a weapon, a spell, or some other means, you have Disadvantage on the roll if you are within 5 feet of an enemy who can see you and doesn’t have the Incapacitated condition (see “Rules Glossary”).
entries.note: Demonstrate each condition: within 5 feet, enemy can see you, enemy not Incapacitated.

entries.name: Melee attacks are within reach

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / Melee Attacks / p. 15

entries.evidence: A melee attack allows you to attack a target within your reach. A melee attack typically uses a handheld weapon or an Unarmed Strike. Many monsters make melee attacks with claws, teeth, or other body parts. A few spells also involve melee attacks.

entries.name: Reach

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / Melee Attacks / Reach / p. 15

crossReferences.unmapped: Creature descriptions (stat blocks) are outside this slice; a greater reach is data the creature supplies.

entries.evidence: A creature has a 5-foot reach and can thus attack targets within 5 feet when making a melee attack. Certain creatures have melee attacks with a reach greater than 5 feet, as noted in their descriptions.

entries.name: Moving past foes provokes an Opportunity Attack

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / Melee Attacks / Opportunity Attacks / p. 15

ambiguity.question: 'If you move heedlessly past your foes' is worded differently from the trigger stated two sentences later ('when a creature that you can see leaves your reach'). Whether it states any further trigger (e.g. moving past a foe without leaving its reach) or only introduces the later one is not fixed.

entries.evidence: Combatants watch for enemies to drop their guard. If you move heedlessly past your foes, you put yourself in danger by provoking an Opportunity Attack.
entries.note: Suspended by the two 'don't provoke' rules, which speak of provoking directly. Mapped rather than declined as prose because it is worded as a condition; the likely reading is that it introduces oa-make.

entries.name: Disengage avoids Opportunity Attacks

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / Melee Attacks / Opportunity Attacks / p. 15

entries.evidence: Avoiding Opportunity Attacks. You can avoid provoking an Opportunity Attack by taking the Disengage action.

entries.name: Teleporting and forced movement don't provoke

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / Melee Attacks / Opportunity Attacks / p. 15

entries.evidence: You also don’t provoke an Opportunity Attack when you Teleport or when you are moved without using your movement, action, Bonus Action, or Reaction. For example, you don’t provoke an Opportunity Attack if an explosion hurls you out of a foe’s reach or if you fall past an enemy.
entries.note: Demonstrate teleport, being moved by an effect, and falling.

entries.name: Making an Opportunity Attack

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / Melee Attacks / Opportunity Attacks / p. 15

entries.evidence: Making an Opportunity Attack. You can make an Opportunity Attack when a creature that you can see leaves your reach. To make the attack, take a Reaction to make one melee attack with a weapon or an Unarmed Strike against that creature. The attack occurs right before it leaves your reach.
entries.note: Trigger: a creature you can see leaves your reach; cost: your Reaction; one melee attack with a weapon or Unarmed Strike; timing: right before it leaves. Suspended while the mover has Disengaged or is teleported or moved without its own movement, while your Reaction is spent, and while you are Incapacitated.

entries.name: What can serve as a mount

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / Mounted Combat / p. 15

ambiguity.question: 'An appropriate anatomy' is not defined and no one is named to decide it, so which willing, larger creatures can serve as a mount is not fixed.

entries.evidence: A willing creature that is at least one size larger than a rider and that has an appropriate anatomy can serve as a mount, using the following rules.
entries.note: 'Willing' and relative size are facts the rule tests. The gate for all mounted entries.

entries.name: Mounting and dismounting

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / Mounted Combat / Mounting and Dismounting / p. 15

entries.evidence: During your move, you can mount a creature that is within 5 feet of you or dismount. Doing so costs an amount of movement equal to half your Speed (round down). For example, if your Speed is 30 feet, you spend 15 feet of movement to mount a horse.
entries.note: Half Speed, round down, for either. Demonstrate an odd Speed.

entries.note: Training is a fact the rule tests; the question is the stated default for 'similar creatures'.

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / Mounted Combat / Controlling a Mount / p. 16

entries.name: Independent mounts

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / Mounted Combat / Controlling a Mount / p. 16

entries.note: DC 10 Dexterity saving throw; on failure, fall off and land Prone.

entries.name: Choosing to attack the rider or the mount

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Combat / Mounted Combat / Controlling a Mount / p. 16

entries.evidence: The Initiative of a controlled mount changes to match yours when you mount it. It moves on your turn as you direct it, and it has only three action options during that turn: Dash, Disengage, and Dodge. A controlled mount can move and act even on the turn that you mount it. In contrast, an independent mount—one that lets you ride but ignores your control—retains its place in the Initiative order and moves and acts as it likes.
